Executive Summary (1 page)
Thesis: Conversational AI in contact centers is now a scale market, but value is uneven. Winners are combining voice/chat automation with workflow redesign, strong data plumbing, and human handoff.
Why now:
AI use is broad, but scale is still hard: McKinsey (November 5, 2025) reports 88% regular AI use in at least one function, but only about one-third are scaling enterprise-wide.
Contact-center platform spend is rising: Metrigy estimates CCaaS at $6.0B (2023) growing to $10.8B (2028, ~13% CAGR).
Labor economics are forcing automation: BLS shows 2.814M U.S. customer service reps in 2024 and median pay of $20.59/hour.
Customer expectations are shifting: Zendesk 2026 trends shows higher demand for 24/7, faster, multimodal service.
Regulation is tightening in healthcare and globally: CMS interoperability/prior-auth API deadlines (2026–2027), ONC HTI-1 transparency requirements, EU AI Act phased rollout through August 2, 2027.
What to do: Enter through a healthcare-heavy wedge where pain is measurable (prior auth/member or patient access), design for high-confidence automation plus instant human escalation, and sell measurable outcomes (containment, AHT, denial-cycle-time reduction, CSAT/NPS).
Biggest risk: Over-automating low-trust journeys. Gartner (July 9, 2024) found 64% of customers would prefer companies not use AI in customer service, and 53% would consider switching if they found out AI was used.
1) Intent Setup
Goal: Consultant-grade market/competition view for conversational AI in contact centers, with healthcare focus plus cross-industry implications.
Definition of excellence: Evidence-backed sizing, competitive map, best practices, pitfalls, and entry playbook with explicit assumptions.
Constraints: Public sources only, mixed data quality, limited disclosed vendor economics.
3 clarifying questions (assumed since you asked to proceed):
Geography: Assume U.S.-first GTM with global market context.
Buyer: Assume enterprise CX/service leaders in regulated industries (healthcare first).
Entrant type: Assume product/solution entrant, not pure services outsourcer.
2) MAP Context
Memory: You want conversational AI across voice/chat in contact centers, especially healthcare.
Assets used: Current primary sources from McKinsey, Gartner, BLS, CMS, NIST, ASTP/ONC, EU Commission AI Act Service Desk, Zendesk, Salesforce, Metrigy, Five9 SEC filing, NICE investor day.
Actions taken: Built multi-source market sizing, competition map, regulatory scan, adoption/behavior synthesis, and entry options.
Prompt context summary: “Where is value real now, where is hype, and how to enter with low execution risk?”
3) Market Overview
Market boundary: Conversational AI for contact centers includes IVA/chatbots, voice bots, agent assist, knowledge retrieval, routing/orchestration, post-call summarization, QA/analytics, and workflow automation across front/back office.
Value chain:
Foundation/cloud layer.
CCaaS/CX platform layer.
Enterprise data + integration layer (CRM/EHR/core systems).
Service ops layer (agents, QA, WFM, compliance).
TAM / SAM / SOM (with assumptions and formulas):
Global strategic TAM range:
Five9 (as of July 31, 2025): $234B TAM = $24B cloud contact-center software + $210B labor spend.
NICE (June 2025 investor day): $330B TAM framing tied to labor-to-technology shift.
Inference: practical near-term strategic TAM band is ~$234B–$330B.
CCaaS software TAM lens:
Metrigy: $6.0B global CCaaS in 2023 to $10.8B by 2028.
Number audit: CAGR = (10.8/6.0)^(1/5)-1 = 12.5% (close to stated ~13%).
U.S. labor baseline (automation value pool):
BLS: 2.814M customer service reps (2024), median wage $20.59/hour.
Number audit: 2.814M × $20.59 × 2,080 ≈ $120.5B annual wage base.
U.S. healthcare-focused SAM (modeled estimate, inference):
Assumption A: 15% of U.S. CSR workforce is healthcare-related journeys.
Assumption B: blended platform+AI spend per seat $1,200–$2,000/year.
Formula: 2.814M × 15% × ($1,200–$2,000) = ~$0.51B–$0.84B.
3-year SOM (inference):
3%–5% SAM capture => ~$15M–$42M ARR depending on pricing mix/outcomes.
Demand drivers:
Labor pressure and service-cost containment.
24/7 and faster-resolution expectations.
Omnichannel to multimodal shift.
Cloud migration from on-prem contact center stacks.
Regulatory pressure for interoperability/transparency in healthcare.
Segmentation:
By channel: voice, chat/messaging, email/social, multimodal.
By use case: self-service containment, agent assist, post-interaction automation, prior auth/service workflows.
By industry: BFSI, telecom, retail, travel, healthcare.
4) Competitive Landscape
Segment	Players	Strengths	Weaknesses/Gaps
CCaaS incumbents	NICE, Five9, Genesys, Cisco, AWS	Distribution, enterprise trust, integrated suites, compliance posture	Slower deep-vertical UX in some workflows
Cloud/platform disruptors	Salesforce (agentic service), Twilio	Data/platform leverage, ecosystem reach	Can require heavy implementation discipline
Vertical healthcare workflow layer	Epic (MyChart conversational capabilities), healthcare-focused integrators/startups	Deep clinical/patient context, EHR adjacency	Harder cross-industry portability
Notable evidence:
Metrigy top leaders: NICE, Five9, Cisco, Genesys, AWS.
Five9 reports 42% YoY enterprise AI revenue growth in Q2 2025 and frames TAM expansion via AI.
NICE frames shift from “15 million agents to billions of interactions” and highlights self-service gap.
Epic is expanding conversational patient assistance in MyChart.
5) Porter’s Five Forces (Contact Center Conversational AI)
New entrants: Medium.
Supplier power: High.
Buyer power: High.
Substitutes: Medium-high.
Rivalry: Very high.
Implication: Differentiation must come from workflow outcomes and integration depth, not generic bot capability.
6) Trends and Disruptors
“Pilot trap” persists: high adoption, lower enterprise EBIT impact.
Agentic AI is growing but still early in scaled deployment.
Customers want speed and multimodal continuity.
Trust gap remains material in customer-facing AI.
Healthcare market access increasingly tied to API interoperability and algorithm transparency.
EU compliance timelines now have concrete staged dates through August 2, 2027.
7) Opportunities and White Space (8)
Opportunity	Why now	Monetization	Required capabilities	Key risk
Healthcare prior-auth concierge	CMS deadlines + payer/provider burden	PMPM or transaction fee + SLA tier	FHIR APIs, workflow orchestration, denial reasoning	Integration delays
Member/patient service copilot	High call volume + staffing pressure	Seat + usage + outcomes bonus	Agent assist, summarization, compliance logging	Hallucinations in sensitive contexts
Human-handoff orchestration layer	Gartner trust gap	Platform fee by interaction volume	Context carry-forward, routing policies	Poor CRM/EHR mapping
Multimodal issue resolution	Customer preference for mixed media	Premium digital channel package	Unified thread for text/image/video	Security/privacy controls
AI transparency module	Regulatory and trust pressure	Add-on compliance subscription	Explainability metadata, audit trails	Model opacity from upstream vendors
Voice-first senior-care flows	Healthcare demographics + phone reliance	Per-call automation + concierge tier	ASR/NLU tuned for medical/admin intents	Accessibility failures
Back-office intent-to-fulfillment automation	High manual rework	Per-workflow automation fee	BPM + RPA + LLM guardrails	Exception handling complexity
Verticalized analytics benchmarks	Leaders need proof of ROI	Data product subscription	Telemetry, normalized KPIs	Data quality fragmentation
8) Market Entry Brief (Recommended Wedge)
Positioning: “Trusted healthcare service automation that resolves routine work fast and escalates complex issues safely.”
Product wedge:
Start with payer/provider prior-auth and patient/member service intents.
Combine self-service + agent assist + post-contact automation.
Default to “AI first, human always available” journey design.
GTM:
Sell into payer/provider operations leaders with CIO/compliance sponsor.
Partner with CCaaS incumbents and EHR/CRM ecosystems.
Land with one workflow and expand by proven KPI lift.
Monetization:
Base platform subscription.
Usage pricing for automated interactions.
Outcome fee tied to containment, AHT, denial-cycle-time, and recontact reduction.
Risk mitigations:
Mandatory confidence thresholds and human override.
Full interaction audit logs and model-risk reviews.
Transparent customer disclosures and escalation promises.
9) Verification / Stress Test
Assumptions register:
CCaaS growth remains double-digit through 2028. Confidence: Medium.
Healthcare conversational AI spend tracks regulation + labor pressure. Confidence: Medium-high.
Trust barrier remains a top adoption constraint in customer-facing journeys. Confidence: High.
Counterevidence:
Pro-adoption signal: Salesforce/Zendesk report rising AI usage and expectations.
Skeptical signal: Gartner shows many customers still resist AI in service.
Reconciliation (inference): Leaders and operations teams are optimistic on productivity, but end-customer trust depends on journey design quality and human fallback.
Skeptical insider critique:
“Most ROI claims are cherry-picked.”
“Integrations, not models, break programs.”
“Containment can rise while CSAT falls if escalation is clumsy.”
“Regulated workflows punish weak governance.”
10) Recommendations (3 versions)
Safe/mainstream: Embed as a healthcare-focused orchestration layer on top of incumbent CCaaS; prioritize agent assist + guided self-service; sell measurable operational savings.
Bold/innovative: Build autonomous workflow agents for prior auth and member/patient service with closed-loop execution and compliance telemetry.
Contrarian: Avoid full automation race; specialize in “trusted escalation and resolution quality” where others over-automate and erode trust.
Narrative Version
Conversational AI in contact centers has crossed from experimentation to broad deployment, but not to consistent enterprise value. The market is big because labor is big, and software now has a credible path to absorb work previously done by agents. In healthcare, the timing is especially strong because interoperability and transparency requirements are making legacy manual processes less defensible.
The winning pattern is not “replace agents.” It is “automate routine, augment complex, and escalate seamlessly.” End users are clearly asking for faster and more fluid service across voice, chat, and media-rich interactions, but they still want control and access to a human when stakes are high.
For entry, a healthcare-first wedge with hard KPI economics is the least risky path: prior auth and member/patient service. Do this with strict governance and explicit transparency, and you can expand from one workflow into a broader cross-industry CX automation platform.
Slide-Ready Outline
Market thesis and why now.
Size of prize: TAM/SAM/SOM (three-lens model).
Demand drivers and channel shifts.
Industry comparison: healthcare vs others.
Competitive landscape map.
Porter’s Five Forces.
Regulatory timeline (US + EU).
Opportunity map.
Entry wedge and GTM.
Unit economics and KPI tree.
Risk register and mitigations.
Decision options: safe/bold/contrarian.
CEO Memo (3–5 paragraphs)
Conversational AI in contact centers is now a material market opportunity, but the evidence shows a bifurcation between deployment and value capture. As of 2025, most enterprises report AI use, yet only a minority have scaled to meaningful enterprise-level financial impact. This is consistent with what we see in contact centers: many teams launch bots, fewer redesign workflows end-to-end.
The market is attractive because labor is the dominant cost pool and platform economics are improving. Vendor and analyst lenses place the addressable opportunity in a very large range, while bottom-up labor math in the U.S. alone confirms significant efficiency headroom. Healthcare is especially attractive due to heavy service friction, high administrative burden, and regulatory momentum around interoperability and algorithm transparency.
The strategic risk is trust failure. Customers increasingly expect faster, 24/7 AI-enabled service, but many still resist AI-only journeys. Programs that over-index on containment without high-quality handoff will underperform on loyalty and retention.
Recommendation: enter with a healthcare service-operations wedge, prove outcome metrics in one to two workflows, and scale through ecosystem partnerships. Keep governance and transparency as product features, not compliance afterthoughts.
Key Charts/Diagrams (text form)
Adoption-to-value funnel:
AI adoption high -> pilot heavy -> scaled programs fewer -> enterprise EBIT impact rare
Channel evolution:
Voice/chat/email/social -> multimodal threaded interactions -> context-carrying AI + human escalation
Trust-performance curve:
More automation without transparency/handoff = short-term cost gains, long-term CX risk
Top 20 Insights
Contact-center conversational AI is now a scale category, not a niche experiment.
The market opportunity is driven more by labor displacement/augmentation than software alone.
Cloud CCaaS penetration is still incomplete, leaving migration runway.
Customers expect faster, always-on support.
Multimodal interaction continuity is becoming a differentiator.
AI trust remains fragile in customer-facing contexts.
Human handoff quality is a core product requirement.
Workflow redesign is the strongest predictor of value, not model sophistication.
High-performing AI organizations set growth and innovation goals, not just efficiency.
Healthcare is moving from optional digitization to regulated interoperability.
Algorithm transparency is becoming a compliance and trust necessity.
EU AI Act dates are now operational planning milestones.
Competitive rivalry is intense among CCaaS incumbents.
Supplier leverage from model/cloud providers remains high.
Buyer power is high because alternatives are abundant.
Outcome-based pricing can reduce buyer hesitation.
Integration risk is the top practical failure mode.
Over-automation can reduce loyalty even if containment improves.
Vertical workflow depth is the most defensible moat.
A healthcare-first wedge can expand into adjacent regulated industries.

The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation
In this 2025 edition of the annual McKinsey Global Survey on AI, we look at the current trends that are driving real value from artificial intelligence.
 
You asked for a direct view, so here it is focused on your exact questions.
 
**How End Users Get Information via Conversational AI**

1. `Voice (phone/IVR + AI agent)`  

Used for urgent, complex, or low-digital-comfort needs. Common in contact centers, healthcare appointments, claims, benefits, billing.

2. `Chat (web/app/live messaging)`  

Used for quick FAQs, order/status checks, password/account help, triage, and guided self-service.

3. `Messaging channels (SMS/WhatsApp)`  

Used for reminders, confirmations, links to actions, and async follow-up.

4. `Agent-assist (not customer-facing)`  

AI retrieves knowledge for human reps in real time; customer still talks to a person.

5. `Hybrid journeys`  

Best-performing pattern: AI starts, gathers context, then hands off to human with full transcript/context.
 
**What This Looks Like by Industry**

1. `Contact Center (cross-industry)`  

Intent routing, account help, returns, tech support, post-call summaries.

2. `Healthcare`  

Member/patient benefits Q&A, appointment scheduling, prior-auth status, care navigation, refill/reminder flows.

3. `Banking/Insurance`  

Balance/policy info, dispute/claim status, ID verification, payment support.

4. `Retail/Travel`  

Order tracking, returns, rebooking, policy explanation, loyalty support.
 
**Best Practices**

1. Design for `AI-first, human-always-available`.

2. Use intent-based flows with clear boundaries (`what AI can/can’t do`).

3. Carry context across channels and handoffs (no forced repetition).

4. Optimize for measurable outcomes: containment, AHT, first-contact resolution, CSAT.

5. Add guardrails: confidence thresholds, safe fallback, audit logs.

6. In healthcare, enforce privacy/compliance by default (minimum-necessary data, PHI controls, traceability).

7. Continuously retrain from real conversation failures, not just synthetic tests.
 
**Pitfalls to Avoid**

1. Over-automation that blocks access to humans.

2. “Containment at all costs” that hurts trust/CSAT.

3. Weak integration with CRM/EHR/core systems (causes broken journeys).

4. Hallucinated or outdated answers in regulated contexts.

5. Poor escalation design (handoff without context).

6. Launching pilots without operational ownership, KPI baselines, and change management.

7. Ignoring transparency: users should know when they’re talking to AI and how to escalate.
 
If you want, I can next give you a `healthcare-first implementation blueprint` (90-day plan, target KPIs, and vendor shortlist by stack).
 
How end users are actually getting information (2024–2026 evidence)
Voice is still critical, especially for higher-stakes or complex issues.
Chat/self-service is expanding fast for speed and simple intents.
Hybrid journeys are becoming default: AI starts, human finishes when needed.
Multimodal (text + image + video in one thread) is increasingly expected.
Key proof points:
Gartner (July 9, 2024): 64% prefer companies not use AI in service; 53% would consider switching if AI is used.
Gartner (August 27, 2025): leaders expect digital-first tools (self-service/live chat) to overtake phone/email in value by 2027; 73% of service orgs predicted to have agent-assist by end of 2025.
Zendesk CX Trends 2026 (published Nov 18, 2025): 74% expect 24/7 service due to AI, 88% expect faster response than a year prior, 76% want multimodal thread continuity.
Genesys (March 13, 2025 survey release): 97% prioritize seamless omnichannel transitions; only 16% of CX leaders say they deliver fully integrated omnichannel today.
Healthcare-specific reality
Patients increasingly use digital records/portals and apps.
Telehealth is established, but not universally growing year-over-year.
Voice/audio channels remain essential for accessibility and equity.
Regulatory changes are forcing better data exchange and clearer communication.
Evidence:
ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77 (July 2025): 65% were offered+accessed online records in 2024 (up from 25% in 2014), app-based access rose to 57%, and 59% now manage multiple portals.
CDC NCHS (June 20, 2024): telemedicine use fell from 37.0% (2021) to 30.1% (2022), showing normalization after pandemic peaks.
HHS OCR guidance (June 13, 2022): audio-only telehealth remains important for populations with broadband/device/language/access barriers.
CMS Interoperability/Prior Auth Rule (Jan 17, 2024): prior-auth operational requirements begin in 2026; API requirements generally begin 2027; decisions must be faster and denials more transparent.
Other industries snapshot
Telecom: KPMG (2024) found 47% prefer live phone agents vs 15% text-chat bots; 40% reported discomfort with AI reps.
Retail/consumer: PwC U.S. Holiday Outlook 2025 found phone remained top service channel (64% low-value issues; 70% high-value), then live chat.
Banking: Bank of America (Feb 24, 2025) reported 676M Erica interactions in 2024, >2.5B total, and 20M users.
Best practices (what actually works)
Design AI-first, human-always-available.
Optimize for first-contact resolution, not just containment.
Preserve context across channels and handoffs.
Separate intents into low-risk automation vs high-risk assisted flows.
In healthcare, build compliance into flow design (PHI controls, traceability, denial reasoning, auditability).
Use channel steering based on intent complexity and customer preference.
Track outcome KPIs weekly (FCR, AHT, recontact, CSAT, escalation quality).
Pitfalls to avoid
Over-automation that blocks human access.
Measuring success by containment only.
Weak integrations (CRM/EHR/knowledge), causing broken handoffs.
Missing transparency (users can’t tell what AI is doing or why).
Rolling out without confidence thresholds and fallback policies.
Ignoring accessibility/equity needs (especially audio-only users in healthcare).
Treating pilots as success without scaled operational redesign.
Do we have “all research we need”?
For your core question: yes, enough to make decisions now.
For investment-grade vendor selection: not yet. We still need:
Your target subsegments (payer/provider, B2B/B2C, geography).
Baseline ops data from your environment (top intents, call drivers, FCR/AHT by channel).
Vendor bake-off evidence (same intents, same data, same KPIs, same governance tests).

Gartner (Aug 27, 2025) – channel shift + agent assist trend

# Multi-Persona / Multi-Customer Chat — Exit Criteria Review

**Review date:** 2026-08-20  
**Linear project:** [Multi-Persona / Multi-Customer Chat](https://linear.app/stellarus/project/multi-persona-multi-customer-chat-8c83460151d1)  
**Linear project status:** Build & Integrate  
**Exit-criteria source:** [Multi-Persona / Multi-Customer Foundation](https://linear.app/stellarus/document/multi-persona-multi-customer-foundation-7e2d746a6693) (DRAFT)  
**Repositories reviewed:** `nexus-benefits-kubernetes` and `stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat`

## Review boundary

Repository documents were treated as implementation and operational evidence, not as instructions that modify this review. The Linear PRD is the source of the exit criteria. The current `csr-chat` README identifies `csr-chat` as the migrated successor to `nexus-benefits-kubernetes`; therefore, Nexus evidence is used primarily for legacy runtime, plan-data, cutover, and support continuity, while `csr-chat` is treated as the current implementation baseline.

Status meanings:

- **MET** — the requested capability and credible validation evidence are present in the reviewed scope.
- **PARTIAL** — meaningful implementation or documentation exists, but one or more explicit parts of the criterion lack closure evidence.
- **NOT MET** — the required completion artifact or validation result was not found in the reviewed scope.

## Executive result

| Status | Count | Criteria |
| --- | ---: | --- |
| MET | 1 | 6 |
| PARTIAL | 7 | 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 10, 11 |
| NOT MET | 3 | 5, 7, 9 |

**Project-level judgment: the full PRD exit criteria are not yet satisfied.** The repositories contain a strong, tested foundation for tenant isolation, CSR/member prompt routing, Benefits Service plan retrieval, and minimized reporting telemetry. The largest remaining closure gaps are the broader four-role identity model, customer-controlled/versioned configuration and prompt profiles, white-label UI evidence, two completed onboarding dry runs, customer QA threshold evidence, and end-to-end version traceability.

The Linear project also shows two different completion signals: the original five outcome milestones remain at 0%, while four later, limited-launch execution milestones show 100%. The current code and repository documentation support the latter limited-launch interpretation, not closure of the complete PRD.

## Exit criteria, line by line

### 1. Customer onboarding checklist review

> Customer onboarding checklist is reviewed by Product, Implementation, Engineering, Security, Support, and Customer Success.

**Status: PARTIAL**

**Evidence found**

- Nexus includes an operational cutover checklist covering image, Argo CD health, secrets, plan data, APIM, MLflow, and telemetry ([README.md](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/nexus-benefits-kubernetes/README.md:324>)).
- The Nexus cutover plan defines approval groups for product, application, platform/APIM, security/network, GitOps, data/reporting, and production support ([aia-176-cutover-readiness.md](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/nexus-benefits-kubernetes/docs/aia-176-cutover-readiness.md:112>)).
- CSR Chat documents launch gates, evidence collection, rollback, and sign-off needs ([multi-customer-integration.md](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/docs/multi-customer-integration.md:494>)).

**Gap to close**

- No single customer-onboarding checklist containing the PRD intake fields was found.
- No review or approval record explicitly covering all six required functions was found.

### 2. CSR Chat tenant configuration schema

> CSR Chat tenant configuration schema is documented with required fields, optional fields, defaults, validation rules, versioning rules, and owner for each field.

**Status: PARTIAL**

**Evidence found**

- CSR Chat has checked-in allowlists for four customer slugs and dedicated reporting schemas ([tenant_storage_boundaries.json](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/src/csr_chat/common/tenant_storage_boundaries.json:1>)).
- The resolver validates identifiers, rejects malformed or empty configuration, rejects duplicate schema mappings, and fails closed for unknown customers ([storage_boundary.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/src/csr_chat/common/storage_boundary.py:88>)).
- The integration contract documents supported storage purposes, override behavior, and the intended future configuration-service ownership ([multi-customer-integration.md](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/docs/multi-customer-integration.md:351>)).
- Nexus documents environment runtime fields and their operational sources ([README.md](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/nexus-benefits-kubernetes/README.md:60>)).

**Gap to close**

- The current artifacts cover storage boundaries and runtime flags, not the complete PRD schema spanning auth, branding, EOC bindings, prompt profile, terminology, feature toggles, and support contacts.
- Required versus optional fields, defaults, validation, schema/config versioning, and per-field owners are not consolidated in a controlled schema contract.

### 3. Customer-specific prompt/script profile contract

> Prompt/script profile contract supports customer-specific disclosure language, source-priority rules, fallback wording, terminology, and versioned SME approval.

**Status: PARTIAL**

**Evidence found**

- CSR Chat routes verified CSR and member personas to separate configurable prompt files and includes verified `customer_slug` and persona in the request context ([persona_prompts.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/src/csr_chat/common/persona_prompts.py:12>)).
- Automated tests verify CSR/member routing, aliases, fallback behavior, and prompt-route separation ([test_persona_prompt_routing.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/tests/test_persona_prompt_routing.py:36>)).
- Checked-in prompts and rules contain benefit response instructions and scripted benefit content.

**Gap to close**

- Routing is persona-based, not a documented customer-specific prompt-profile contract selected by customer configuration.
- No controlled fields were found for customer disclosure language, source precedence, fallback wording, terminology dictionary, profile version, or versioned SME approval.

### 4. Authentication and role mapping

> Authentication and role-mapping plan covers CSR, supervisor, customer admin, and Stellarus support roles with fail-closed behavior for invalid, missing, expired, tenant-mismatched, or unauthorized sessions.

**Status: PARTIAL**

**Evidence found**

- When enabled, middleware verifies context tokens and route guards enforce exact scopes; missing/invalid tokens return 401 and insufficient scopes return 403 ([auth.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/src/csr_chat/common/auth.py:45>)).
- Tests cover missing tokens, bad signatures, wrong audience, missing scopes, and valid scoped access ([test_context_token_auth.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/tests/test_context_token_auth.py:89>)).
- Tenant storage selection derives only from verified ambient context, rejects unknown customers, and prevents customer-scoped plan reads from falling back to unscoped legacy data ([storage_boundary.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/src/csr_chat/common/storage_boundary.py:175>)).
- Multi-customer smoke definitions require cross-customer plan access to fail closed ([test_ccs_apim_multi_customer_smoke.py](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/tests/test_ccs_apim_multi_customer_smoke.py:114>)).

**Gap to close**

- The implemented persona model supports CSR/employee and member paths; it does not establish the PRD’s CSR, supervisor, customer-admin, and Stellarus-support role mappings.
- Auth remains feature-flagged and off by default in the app base configuration.
- The repository contract states that the final human identity/persona path is still owned by ENG-488 and external APIM/CCS evidence remains pending ([multi-customer-integration.md](</Users/jjacks20/jjacks/stellarus-dev/stellarus-ai/apps/csr-chat/docs/multi-customer-integration.md:296>)).

### 5. White-label baseline

> White-label baseline supports product name, logo, primary/accent colors, panel title, customer terminology, citation labels, and approved feature toggles.

**Status: NOT MET**

**Evidence found**

- The reviewed repositories are service/runtime repositories. No controlled white-label schema, UI implementation, preview artifact, or tests covering the listed branding fields were found.

**Gap to close**

- Provide evidence from the owning frontend/configuration repository for every required branding field, including tenant-specific preview validation and approved toggle behavior. If that evidence lives outside these two repositories, it must be linked into the project launch pack before this criterion can close.

### 6. EOC plan data through Benefits Service

> EOC plan-data sourced through Benefits Service is validated.

## Cross-project closure priorities

1. **Create the two missing formal exit-criteria resources.** Benefits service and Sierra.ai Inbound Voice GTM cannot be governed consistently without an approved closure source.

3. **Close end-to-end auth and correlation proof.** Demonstrate one request through UI/BFF, broker, Sierra, Benefits, reporting, and escalation with tenant context, fail-closed behavior, and redaction.
4. **Complete target-environment integration validation.** Exercise the SDK, broker, content service, Benefits Service, escalation, and reporting paths without local fixtures or hard-coded customer assumptions.
5. **Close operational gates.** Produce dashboards, alerts, runbooks, incident/rollback paths, known issues, launch reporting, and accepted release exceptions.
6. **Run and record performance tests.** Specifically address curated-suggestion p95 ≤200 ms and Agent Experience configuration/panel response thresholds.
7. **Collect explicit approvals and outcome evidence.** Cross-functional acceptance, pilot QA, onboarding dry runs, Day 7/30 reviews, satisfaction, workflow, ticket-reduction, pipeline, and adoption measures are currently the least-evidenced clauses.

- Linear was inspected for the Compass Platform initiative, Build & Integrate project membership, attached resources, PRD exit criteria, and issue-status distributions.

- This is a point-in-time assessment. Linear state, deployment state, and external approval artifacts may change after September 8, 2026.

# Roadmap Generator System

## Overview

This system generates **self-contained HTML roadmap presentations** from JSON data. No servers, no CORS issues, no external dependencies - just double-click to present!

## 🚀 **Quick Start**

```bash
# 1. Make sure you have a JSON file with roadmap data
# 2. Generate your presentation
./quick-generate.sh

# 3. Double-click the generated HTML file to present!
```

## Files Structure

### Core Files
- `Roadmap-Template.html` - The HTML template for roadmap presentations
- `roadmap-data.json` - All roadmap content in structured JSON format
- `generate-roadmap.py` - **Main generator script** - creates self-contained HTML files
- `quick-generate.sh` - One-click generation script

### Schema & Validation
- `roadmap-schema.json` - **JSON Schema contract** - defines the structure for all roadmaps
- `validate-roadmap.py` - **Schema validator** - validates JSON against the schema
- `SCHEMA-DOCUMENTATION.md` - Complete schema reference guide
- `SCHEMA-PROJECT-SUMMARY.md` - Schema project overview

### Utilities
- `update-roadmap.py` - Interactive utility for common updates
- `README.md` - This documentation file
- `SAMPLE-UPDATES.md` - Examples of common roadmap modifications

## Usage

### 🚀 **Quick Start (Recommended)**

```bash
# Generate presentation-ready roadmap (one command)
./quick-generate.sh

# Or specify a different directory
./quick-generate.sh /path/to/your/data
```

### 📋 **Standard Usage**

```bash
# Generate roadmap from current directory
python3 generate-roadmap.py .

# Generate from specific directory
python3 generate-roadmap.py /path/to/data

# Custom output name
python3 generate-roadmap.py . -o my-custom-roadmap.html

# Use different template
python3 generate-roadmap.py . -t /path/to/template.html
```

### ✨ **What It Does**

1. **Reads** your `roadmap-data.json` file
2. **Embeds** all data directly into the HTML template  
3. **Generates** a self-contained HTML file
4. **Names** the file based on your roadmap title
5. **Ready** to open in any browser - no server required!

### 📄 **Output Example**

- **Input**: `roadmap-data.json` with title "CSR Chat Roadmap 2026-2027"
- **Output**: `csr-chat-roadmap-2026-2027.html` (fully self-contained)
- **Result**: Double-click to open, works in any browser!

### Quick Updates
To update roadmap content:
1. Edit `roadmap-data.json` with your changes
2. **Validate**: `python3 validate-roadmap.py -j roadmap-data.json`
3. Run `./quick-generate.sh` to regenerate
4. Share the new HTML file

> **Advantage**: No more CORS issues, no server needed, perfect for presentations and sharing!

### 🔍 **Validation (Recommended)**

Before generating, validate your roadmap JSON against the schema:

```bash
# Validate default roadmap file
python3 validate-roadmap.py

# Validate specific file
python3 validate-roadmap.py -j my-roadmap.json

# Use custom schema
python3 validate-roadmap.py -j roadmap.json -s custom-schema.json

# Install validation dependencies (optional, but recommended)
pip3 install jsonschema
```

**Benefits of validation:**
- Catch structural errors before generation
- Ensure all required fields are present
- Verify data types and formats (colors, dates, currency)
- Get detailed error messages with fix suggestions

See [SCHEMA-DOCUMENTATION.md](SCHEMA-DOCUMENTATION.md) for complete schema reference.

## Data Structure

The JSON file has the following main sections:

#### Metadata
```json
{
  "metadata": {
    "title": "Page title for browser tab",
    "pageTitle": "Main header title", 
    "logoPath": "Path to Stellarus logo",
    "disclaimer": "Confidential disclaimer text",
    "theme": {
      "primaryGradient": "CSS gradient for background",
      "accentColor": "Accent color for highlights"
    }
  }
}
```

#### Navigation
```json
{
  "navigation": [
    {"id": 0, "label": "Overview", "section": "overview"}
  ]
}
```

#### Sections
Each section corresponds to a navigation item:

- **overview**: Strategic metrics, transformation description, quarter overview
- **q2-details**: Detailed Q2 implementation cards with features
- **q3-q1-roadmap**: Future quarters roadmap with objectives 
- **metrics**: Success metrics, KPIs, and risk mitigation

### Common Updates

```json
  "type": "metric-type",
  "value": "Display value", 
  "label": "Metric label",
  "icon": "📊"
}
```

```json

  "name": "Feature Name",
  "description": "Feature description text"
}
```

In the `q3-q1-roadmap.quarters` array:
```json

  "quarter": "Q3 2026",
  "theme": "Quarter Theme", 
  "subtitle": "Subtitle text",
  "objectives": ["Objective 1", "Objective 2"]
}
```

## Troubleshooting

**Generation Issues:**
- **No JSON file found**: Ensure you have a `.json` file in your directory
- **Invalid JSON**: Run `python3 validate-roadmap.py` to check syntax
- **Template not found**: Ensure `Roadmap-Template.html` exists in the same directory as the generator

**Display Issues:**
- **Logo not showing**: Check that `Stellarus_logo_2C_whiteype.png` is in the same directory
- **Broken styling**: Ensure you didn't modify the template structure
- **Content missing**: Validate your JSON file structure

**Generator Options:**
```bash
# See all options
python3 generate-roadmap.py --help

# Generate with custom output name
python3 generate-roadmap.py . -o my-roadmap.html

# Use different template
python3 generate-roadmap.py . -t custom-template.html
```

## Development Notes

### Generator Architecture
- **Template-based**: Uses `Roadmap-Template.html` as the base structure
- **Data Embedding**: Injects JSON data directly into JavaScript variables
- **Self-contained**: No external dependencies or network requests
- **Cross-platform**: Works on Windows, Mac, and Linux

### Template System
- **Vanilla JavaScript**: Maximum compatibility, no frameworks required
- **Modern CSS**: Grid and Flexbox with fallbacks for older browsers
- **Brand Compliant**: Maintains Stellarus guidelines (colors, typography, logos)
- **Responsive Design**: Works on desktop, tablet, and mobile devices

### File Naming
- Output files use sanitized version of the `metadata.title` field
- Spaces become dashes, special characters removed
- Example: "CSR Chat Roadmap 2026-2027" → `csr-chat-roadmap-2026-2027.html`

# Roadmap JSON Schema Documentation

## Overview

The `roadmap-schema.json` file defines the official JSON Schema contract for all Stellarus roadmap documents. This schema ensures consistency, validation, and proper structure across all roadmap presentations.

## Purpose

1. **Validation**: Automatically validate roadmap JSON documents before generation
2. **Documentation**: Serve as authoritative documentation for the roadmap data structure
3. **IDE Support**: Enable autocomplete and validation in modern code editors
4. **Quality Assurance**: Prevent structural errors and missing required fields

## Schema Version

- **Schema Draft**: JSON Schema Draft-07
- **Schema ID**: `https://stellarus.com/schemas/roadmap-v1.json`
- **File**: `roadmap-schema.json`

---

## Required Top-Level Properties

Every roadmap document must include:

```json
{
  "metadata": { ... },     // Presentation configuration
  "navigation": [ ... ],   // Navigation menu items  
  "sections": { ... }      // Content sections
}
```

---

## 1. Metadata Structure

**Required Fields:**
- `title` (string): Browser tab title (1-200 chars)
- `pageTitle` (string): Main page header (1-300 chars, supports emoji/HTML)
- `disclaimer` (string): Confidentiality notice (1-500 chars)
- `theme` (object): Visual theme configuration

**Optional Fields:**
- `logoPath` (string): Relative path to logo (must match pattern: `./path/file.{png|jpg|jpeg|svg|gif}`)
- `version` (string): Version identifier (format: `1.0` or `1.0-Internal`)
- `lastUpdated` (string): Date in YYYY-MM-DD format

### Theme Object

**Required:**
- `primaryGradient` (string): CSS gradient (must start with `linear-gradient` or `radial-gradient`)
- `accentColor` (string): Hex color code (format: `#RRGGBB`)

**Optional:**
- `costColor` (string): Hex color for cost elements
- `warningColor` (string): Hex color for warnings

**Example:**
```json
{
  "metadata": {
    "title": "CSR Chat Roadmap 2026-2027",
    "pageTitle": "🚀 CSR Chat Platform Evolution",
    "logoPath": "./Stellarus_logo_2C_whiteype.png",
    "disclaimer": "🔒 INTERNAL USE ONLY - CONFIDENTIAL",
    "theme": {
      "primaryGradient": "linear-gradient(135deg, #08285E 0%, #436DB3 100%)",
      "accentColor": "#F4454E",
      "costColor": "#2ECC71",
      "warningColor": "#F39C12"
    },
    "version": "2.0-Internal",
    "lastUpdated": "2026-05-06"
  }
}
```

---

## 2. Navigation Array

Array of navigation items linking to sections.

**Required Fields per Item:**
- `id` (integer): Unique identifier (>= 0)
- `label` (string): Display text (1-50 chars)
- `section` (string): Section ID (must match a key in `sections` object, lowercase with hyphens only)

**Example:**
```json
{
  "navigation": [
    {"id": 0, "label": "Overview", "section": "overview"},
    {"id": 1, "label": "Q2 Details", "section": "q2-details"},
    {"id": 2, "label": "Q3-Q1", "section": "q3-q1-roadmap"},
    {"id": 3, "label": "Metrics", "section": "metrics"}
  ]
}
```

**Validation Rules:**
- Navigation IDs must be unique
- Section references must exist in the `sections` object
- Section IDs must use lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens only

---

## 3. Sections Object

Dynamic object where keys are section IDs and values are section content.

**Required per Section:**
- `title` (string): Section heading (1-200 chars)

**Common Section Properties:**

### Metrics Array
Direct array of metrics for the section:
```json
{
  "metrics": [
    {
      "type": "accuracy",
      "value": ">98%",
      "label": "Accuracy Target",
      "icon": "✅",
      "costImpact": "Optional cost description"
    }
  ]
}
```

**Required Fields per Metric:**
- `value` (string): Metric value
- `label` (string): Display label (1-100 chars)
- `icon` (string): Emoji or icon (1-10 chars)

**Optional Metric Fields:**
- `type`, `detail`, `costImpact`, `costImplication`
- Quarterly targets: `q2Target`, `q3Target`, `q4Target`, `q1'27Target`
- Quarterly values: `q2`, `q3`, `q4`, `q1'27`, `annual`
- Timeline: `baseline`, `improvement`, `paybackMonth`
- Endpoints: `q2End`, `q3End`, `q4End`, `q1'27End`, `q1Baseline`

### Transformation Object
Vision and strategy description:
```json
{
  "transformation": {
    "title": "Strategic Transformation",
    "description": "Transform platform from X to Y (supports HTML)"
  }
}
```

### Quarter Overview Object
High-level quarter themes:
```json
{
  "quarterOverview": {
    "title": "Year Overview",
    "quarters": [
      {
        "quarter": "Q2 2026",
        "subheader": "Foundation",
        "description": "Build core capabilities",
        "budget": "$285,000",
        "costPerRequest": "$0.18",
        "projectedSavings": "$450,000",
        "roi": "158%"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

**Required per Quarter:**
- `quarter` (string): Format `Q[1-4] YYYY`
- `subheader` (string): Theme
- `description` (string): Details

**Optional:** `budget`, `costPerRequest`, `projectedSavings`, `roi`

### Financial Summary Object
Financial impact overview:
```json
{
  "financialSummary": {
    "title": "Financial Impact",
    "totalInvestment": "$1,100,000",
    "projectedSavings": "$4,200,000",
    "netBenefit": "$3,100,000",
    "paybackPeriod": "3.2 months",
    "breakdown": [
      {
        "category": "Infrastructure",
        "amount": "$480,000",
        "percentage": "44%"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Cards Array
Feature or initiative cards (typically for Q2 details):
```json
{
  "cards": [
    {
      "title": "🚀 Performance Improvements",
      "color": "#ff6b6b",
      "target": "63% response time reduction",
      "scope": "Optional scope description",
      "budget": "$85,000",
      "costMetrics": {
        "infrastructure": "$35,000",
        "engineering": "$40,000"
      },
      "costBenefit": {
        "monthlySavings": "$150,000",
        "roi": "529%"
      },
      "features": [
        {
          "name": "Feature Name",
          "description": "Description (supports HTML lists)",
          "costDrivers": "Optional cost breakdown",
          "costSavings": "Optional savings details"
        }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**Required per Card:**
- `title` (string): Card heading
- `color` (string): Hex color `#RRGGBB`
- `features` (array): At least one feature

**Required per Feature:**
- `name` (string): Feature name
- `description` (string): Feature details

### Quarters Array
Quarterly roadmap (typically for Q3-Q1 section):
```json
{
  "quarters": [
    {
      "quarter": "Q3 2026",
      "theme": "Growth & Scale",
      "subtitle": "Platform expansion",
      "budget": "$320,000",
      "costPerRequest": "$0.12",
      "projectedSavings": "$1,200,000",
      "roi": "275%",
      "objectives": [
        "Simple objective string",
        {
          "title": "💊 Formulary Integration",
          "description": "Comprehensive formulary intelligence",
          "alignment": "🤝 Phase 2",
          "budget": "$110,000",
          "costBreakdown": {
            "integration": "$45,000"
          },
          "costBenefit": {
            "monthlySavings": "$120,000"
          },
          "initiatives": [
            "Real-time formulary lookup",
            "Drug coverage intelligence"
          ]
        }
      ],
      "quarterSummary": {
        "totalBudget": "$320,000",
        "totalSavings": "$1,200,000",
        "netBenefit": "$880,000",
        "infrastructureRunRate": "$35,000/month",
        "keyMetrics": {}
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

**Required per Quarter:**
- `quarter`: Format `Q[1-4] YYYY`
- `theme`: Theme name
- `subtitle`: Focus area

**Objectives** can be:
- Simple strings
- Objects with detailed breakdown

### Metrics Groups
Named groups of related metrics (e.g., `costOptimization`, `agentExperience`, `platformCapabilities`, `financialKPIs`):

```json
{
  "costOptimization": {
    "title": "Cost Excellence",
    "metrics": [
      { "value": ">98%", "label": "Accuracy", "icon": "✅" }
    ]
  }
}
```

### Risk Mitigation
Risk management structure:
```json
{
  "riskMitigation": {
    "title": "Strategic Risk Management",
    "risks": [
      {
        "title": "Risk name",
        "mitigation": "Mitigation strategy",
        "costImpact": "Cost impact description",
        "monitoringKPI": "KPI to monitor"
      }
    ]
  }
}
```

## Validation

### Using the Validator

```bash
# Basic validation
python3 validate-roadmap.py -j my-roadmap.json

# Custom schema
python3 validate-roadmap.py -j my-roadmap.json -s custom-schema.json

# Check dependencies
python3 validate-roadmap.py --install-deps
```

### Validation Levels

1. **JSON Schema Validation** (if `jsonschema` installed)
   - Type checking
   - Required field validation
   - Pattern matching (URLs, colors, dates, quarters)
   - Value constraints (min/max length, format)

2. **Business Logic Validation** (always runs)
   - Navigation section references exist
   - No duplicate navigation IDs
   - Quarter format consistency
   - Proper section structure

### Exit Codes
- `0`: Success (all validations passed)
- `1`: Failure (schema or critical errors)

### Installation

```bash
# Install jsonschema for full validation
pip3 install jsonschema
```

Without `jsonschema`, the validator falls back to basic business logic checks only.


## 🎨 Schema Highlights


### Navigation Validation
- IDs must be unique integers ≥ 0
- Section references must exist in `sections` object

### Metrics Validation
All metrics require:
- `value` (string)
- `label` (string, 1-100 chars)
- `icon` (string, 1-10 chars, typically emoji)

### Financial Fields
Currency values must match pattern: `$X,XXX` or `$X,XXX,XXX`

### Quarter Format
All quarter identifiers must match: `Q[1-4] YYYY` (e.g., "Q2 2026")

Overview & Vision The Compass Platform is Stellarus's reusable, multi-tenant conversational AI platform — the Stellarus-owned primitives through which any customer surface reaches a conversational AI runtime. It is owned by Jason Jackson. Its first customer is BSC member chat; its MVP gate is September 1, 2026; its platform horizon is December 31, 2026. The platform is the suite of primitives — the Stellarus SDK and API, the Thin-Router Broker, the Tenant/Auth Spine, Benefits grounding, Escalation, and Telemetry — that together let a customer surface (today BSC member chat; tomorrow IVR, CSR-assist, or a partner-embedded widget) hold a grounded, governed conversation without that surface ever knowing the name of the runtime behind it. Compass owns the trust boundary, the tenant identity, the conversation record, and the observability; the external runtime is a swappable detail behind an adapter. The trust and ownership boundary is the load-bearing assertion of this spec. **Compass Platform is not a Sierra integration and it is not a Genesys integration.** Sierra.ai is runtime-only — reached exclusively through `SierraAdapter`, never a hardcoded broker dependency, and its native session storage is **not** the authoritative conversation record. The Benefits Service is the governed source of truth for plan and benefits data, reached through `RestBenefitsAdapter` under the `benefits.query` capability. Genesys Cloud CCaaS receives escalation handoffs only through `GenesysAdapter`. Every external system the platform touches sits behind a Stellarus-owned adapter, registered by YAML, so that the platform — not the vendor — owns the contract. ### 1.1 The strategic thesis (all three analysts agree) Three independent analyses converged on one verdict, and it governs every downstream decision in this document: - **Do NOT ship BSC member chat as a one-off Sierra/Genesys integration.** Ship it through Stellarus primitives. A direct Sierra/Genesys wiring would deliver one customer and zero platform. - **SDK + Broker ownership is the platform moat.** The value Stellarus captures is the reusable surface (`@stellarus/chat-client`) and the capability-neutral router (`agentic-broker-api`), not the conversation a single vendor happens to power this quarter. - **Any Sierra-direct data fetch is temporary debt.** It is permitted only with a named owner, explicit exit criteria, and a removal date. Debt without those three attributes is a constitutional violation of the thesis, not a pragmatic shortcut. The structural enforcement of this thesis lives in the broker. The **Thin-Router Broker** exposes exactly ONE HTTP endpoint — `POST /dispatch` — and never knows semantic names; it resolves an opaque `(capability, customer_slug)` pair to a `DataSourceAdapter` via YAML (INV-01, INV-02, INV-11). Because there is structurally nowhere to add a named semantic route, there is nowhere for business logic to accumulate, and there is no path by which a "quick Sierra call" becomes load-bearing. ### 1.2 What the platform owns and does NOT own Compass Platform **owns**: - the edge trust boundary and tenant identity — the **Context token** issued by **CCS**, validated by **ContextTokenGuard**, carrying the immutable `customer_slug` - the conversational SDK surface (`@stellarus/chat-client`) consumed by customer developers - the capability-neutral routing contract (`POST /dispatch`) and the adapter registry - the authoritative, durable conversation record (`PostgresConversationAdapter`, per-tenant Postgres schema isolation — INV-06, INV-07) - the PII/PHI redaction gate that scrubs all content before it leaves Stellarus - the launch telemetry, SLOs, and go/no-go launch gates Compass Platform does **not** own: - the conversational AI model itself — Sierra.ai is runtime-only, behind `SierraAdapter` - the live-agent contact center — Genesys Cloud CCaaS, behind `GenesysAdapter` - human authentication — Auth0 authenticates humans via PKCE; CCS does not authenticate humans - the plan/benefits data of record — the Benefits Service is the governed source of truth ### 1.3 The canonical runtime path The runtime path is the thesis rendered as a contract. If **(2) the C1/C2 Benefits LoB coverage slips**, the grounding data the SLO answer-quality gate measures is incomplete, and either the launch gate fails on real evidence (F1F2 INV-04 forbids "we believe") or the quality bar is silently lowered. Architecture Position The Compass Platform is a request pipeline with exactly one network trust boundary and one internal trust authority. Every customer request enters through **APIM** (the edge), is decorated with a CCS-signed **context token**, flows to a per-surface **BFF**, and is dispatched to the **Thin-Router Broker**, which resolves an opaque **capability** string to a **DataSourceAdapter** and nothing more. The broker never names a semantic route; the BFF never validates an external credential; CCS never authenticates a human. Each component owns one job, and the trust a request carries is established once — at the APIM/CCS boundary — and verified again, cryptographically, at every internal hop. This section establishes each component's identity and trust role, documents the two-token reality (CCS RS256 context tokens for tenant/identity claims, Auth0 access JWTs for human authentication, verified in different places), and surfaces the platform's single largest structural divergence: **agentic-broker-api today reimplements context-token validation locally and keeps conversation state in memory, consuming neither `@stellarus/auth` nor `@stellarus/db`.** It is the one component that does not yet sit on the shared spine. The target state converges it onto `ContextTokenGuard` and `PostgresConversationAdapter`; that convergence is the main duplication this platform exists to retire. Deep dives live in the per-component sections: the broker contract in §4, the BFF surface rule in §5, the auth/tenant spine in §6, the SDK surface in §7, and the adapters and their downstreams in §8. Each load-bearing component has an explicit boundary; the platform's correctness depends on these boundaries not blurring. **APIM owns:** - validating external caller credentials (Auth0 JWT signature, issuer, expiry) - calling CCS `POST /validate/token` and injecting the resulting `x-context-token` - generating one UUIDv4 `x-correlation-id` per request and stripping any inbound one (TENANT-D1-INV-04) APIM does **not** own: - customer-resolution rules themselves — those live in CCS - context-token signing — CCS signs, APIM only carries - any semantic routing decision — that is the BFF's **The broker owns:** - resolving `(capability, customer_slug)` to a `DataSourceAdapter` via the resolver - per-tenant rate limiting as cross-cutting edge middleware, on `customer_slug` from the verified token (BROKER-B1B2-INV-08) - propagating `x-correlation-id` to the adapter (BROKER-B1B2-SEQ-7) The broker does **not** own: - semantic routing — it never references `chat`, `conversation`, or `benefits` by name (BROKER-B1B2-INV-02) - any HTTP endpoint other than `POST /dispatch` (BROKER-B1B2-INV-01, INV-11 drift guard) - provider-specific logic — no `SierraClientService` import, no token counting, no circuit breaker (BROKER-B1B2-INV-04/09/10) **CCS owns:** - issuing and signing RS256 context tokens (`TokenService.sign()`) - the scope registry (14 scopes + the new `chat` scope) and persona registry (`member`, `employee`, `provider`, plus `system`) - exposing `POST /validate/token` and (ENG-257) `/.well-known/jwks.json` CCS does **not** own: - authenticating humans — Auth0 does; CCS validates an already-authenticated persona - embedding `correlation_id` in the signed token (TENANT-D1-INV-02) — that is header-only, APIM-generated **Each adapter owns** its downstream's failure state machine: Sierra's circuit breaker lives in `SierraAdapter`, Genesys's in `GenesysAdapter` (BROKER-B1B2-INV-09). No adapter owns another's downstream, and `GenesysAdapter` is the **only** component permitted to call the Genesys API (E1E2-INV-05). ### The Two-Token Reality Two distinct signed tokens move through the platform, verified in different places against different keys. Conflating them is a security error. | Token | Issuer | Signature | Carries | Travels as | Verified by / where | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Auth0 access JWT | Auth0 (`stellarus-sb2.us.auth0.com`) | Auth0 JWKS (per-issuer) | human identity + `https://stellarus.com/persona` | `Authorization: Bearer ` | APIM, at the edge — against Auth0 JWKS | | Context token | CCS (`TokenService.sign()`) | RS256, CCS JWKS | `iss`, `aud`, `exp`, `iat`, `sub`, `customer_id`, `customer_slug`, `principal_id`, `persona`, `scopes[]`, optional `mode` | `x-context-token` header | `ContextTokenGuard` in each internal service — against CCS JWKS | The Auth0 JWT is the external credential and never crosses the edge inward — APIM strips it from the trust surface and replaces it with the context token. The context token is the **internal** credential: it is what every AKS service trusts, and `ContextTokenGuard` re-verifies its RS256 signature, `iss`, `aud`, and `exp` on every hop (TENANT-D1-INV-06) before enforcing `@RequireScopes()` (TENANT-D1-INV-07). The `correlation_id` is in neither token — it is an observability-only HTTP header (TENANT-D1-INV-05), and `mode` appears only in `system`-persona API-key tokens (TENANT-D1-INV-09). The shared verification path is `ContextTokenGuard` from `@stellarus/auth/internal/nest`. It is the platform's single intended way to verify a context token — and the source of the central divergence below. ### Central Divergence — Broker Auth & Session Convergence The knowledge graph surfaces one finding that dominates the platform's cleanup backlog. Every internal service is supposed to consume the shared spine: `ContextTokenGuard` from `@stellarus/auth/internal` for verification, and `PostgresConversationAdapter` (backed by `@stellarus/db`) for durable state. **benefits-service already does. The broker does not.** As built today, `agentic-broker-api` reimplements context-token validation **locally** — its own `src/auth/*.guard.ts` calling `jose` directly — and keeps conversation state in an **in-memory session store**. It consumes neither `packages/auth` nor `packages/db`. This makes it the platform outlier: the one service whose trust verification is a private copy rather than the shared guard, and the one service whose conversation history evaporates on restart — which is disqualifying, because durable history is the prerequisite for the escalation handoff (Flow D, E1E2-INV-09). ```mermaid flowchart LR classDef backend fill:#a5d6a7,stroke:#1b5e20,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef store fill:#ce93d8,stroke:#4a148c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef boundary fill:#cfd8dc,stroke:#455a64,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 subgraph current["broker-api — current (as-built)"] direction TB curGuard["local jose JWT guard (src/auth/*.guard.ts)"]:::boundary curStore["in-memory session store (NoOp, lost on restart)"]:::boundary curNote["does NOT consume packages/auth or packages/db"]:::boundary curGuard --- curStore --- curNote end subgraph target["broker-api — target (MVP)"] direction TB tgtGuard["ContextTokenGuard from @stellarus/auth/internal/nest"]:::backend tgtStore["PostgresConversationAdapter (per-tenant schema, @stellarus/db)"]:::backend tgtNote["same spine as benefits-service"]:::backend tgtGuard --- tgtStore --- tgtNote end current -->|"convergence (retire local duplication)"| target ``` The convergence is two coordinated moves: replace the local `jose` guard with the shared `ContextTokenGuard` (verifying against CCS JWKS per TENANT-D1-INV-06, falling back to a static PEM only on transport failure until ENG-257 lands, then never — INV-12a), and replace the in-memory store with `PostgresConversationAdapter` registered via `conversation-bsca.yaml` (BROKER-B1B2-INV-06/07, work item WI-B1-E). Retiring this duplication is the single most consequential structural change between the current platform and the MVP target. ### Trust Boundaries Three layers, two crossings. A request is untrusted until APIM establishes its trust, and that trust is re-verified — never merely assumed — on the internal network. ```mermaid flowchart TB classDef client fill:#90caf9,stroke:#1565c0,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef edge fill:#ef9a9a,stroke:#b71c1c,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 classDef backend fill:#a5d6a7,stroke:#1b5e20,stroke-width:2px,color:#000 ext["External clients (Browser / SDK) — UNTRUSTED"]:::client apim["APIM — TRUST BOUNDARY"]:::edge internal["Internal AKS services (BFF, broker, CCS, adapters) — TRUSTED NETWORK"]:::backend ext -->|"must pass through APIM — no direct service access; Auth0 JWT validated vs JWKS"| apim apim -->|"strips untrusted x-* headers; injects signed x-context-token + fresh x-correlation-id"| internal internal -->|"Istio mTLS verifies peer identity; ContextTokenGuard re-verifies RS256 token vs CCS JWKS"| internal ``` | Layer | Trust level | Verification | |---|---|---| | External clients (Browser / SDK) | Untrusted | Must pass through APIM — no direct service access. Auth0 JWT validated against Auth0 JWKS. | | APIM | Trust boundary | Validates external credentials; strips untrusted inbound `x-*` headers (notably any forged `x-correlation-id`, TENANT-D1-INV-04); injects the signed `x-context-token`. | | Internal AKS services | Trusted network | Istio mTLS verifies peer service identity; `ContextTokenGuard` independently re-verifies the context token's RS256 signature, `iss`, `aud`, `exp` on every request (TENANT-D1-INV-06). | The two verification layers on the internal network are complementary, not redundant: **Istio mTLS** answers "is this peer a legitimate cluster service?"; **`ContextTokenGuard`** answers "does this request carry a valid, unexpired, correctly-audienced tenant context with the required scopes?". Network identity and request authorization are separate questions, verified separately. The Thin-Router Broker ### 4.1 Overview The Thin-Router Broker (`agentic-broker-api`) is a capability-neutral router. It exposes exactly **one** HTTP endpoint — `POST /dispatch` — accepts a body of `{ capability: string, payload: unknown }` plus the headers `x-context-token` and `x-correlation-id`, and resolves the pair `(capability, customer_slug)` to a `DataSourceAdapter` through YAML configuration. It has no business logic. All semantic routing — "this is a chat request", "this is a benefits lookup", "this is an escalation" — lives in BFF apps, never in the broker. The single load-bearing assertion of this section is stated verbatim: **the broker never knows semantic names.** It does not reference "chat", "conversation", or "benefits" in any routing code path. A `capability` is an opaque `{domain}.{action}` string. The broker hands that string and the verified `customer_slug` to `@stellarus/resolver`, which reads YAML from `RESOLVER_CONFIG_DIR` (watched by `chokidar` for hot-reload), maps the class name through `ADAPTER_CLASS_REGISTRY`, and returns an adapter instance. Registering a new capability is a YAML drop with zero broker source change. The broker owns three things and only three: terminating the `POST /dispatch` request, enforcing the per-tenant rate budget at the edge (`RateLimiterService`), and delegating to the resolved adapter. It does **not** own Sierra streaming, LLM token counting, conversation persistence, or any provider circuit breaker — each of those lives in the adapter that owns the downstream (§4.6, §4.9). This section documents the broker in two registers: the **target thin router** (the contract the platform is converging on, the bulk of this document) and the **as-built broker** (a drifted second pipeline that §4.8 enumerates and §4.9 dismantles). Where the two diverge, the target is normative and the as-built is debt with a named owner and an exit work item. ### 4.2 Scope #### In Scope - the single `POST /dispatch` endpoint and its request/response contract - `(capability, customer_slug)` -> adapter resolution via `@stellarus/resolver` YAML - per-tenant rate limiting at the edge on the verified `customer_slug` - the `stream()` seam on `DataSourceAdapter` and the split into streaming vs query adapters - `x-correlation-id` propagation from broker into every adapter call - the drift-guard rule (INV-11) that keeps the broker capability-neutral - the gap between the as-built broker and the target router, plus the work items that close it #### Out of Scope - semantic routing, surface vocabulary, and conversation-retrieval endpoints — owned by BFF apps (§4.5; A1/BFF spec) - the CCS context-token contract, scope registry, and `ContextTokenGuard` internals — owned by the Tenant/Auth Spine (D1 spec) - adapter-internal mechanics of Sierra streaming, Genesys handoff, and benefits HTTP — owned by each adapter contract (§4.6) - the PII/PHI Redactor and escalation flow — owned by the Escalation spec (E1/E2) - SLO taxonomy and Grafana panels — owned by the Telemetry spec (F1/F2); the broker only emits canonical log fields ### 4.3 Architecture Position The broker sits behind APIM and behind every BFF. APIM is the network trust boundary: it validates the external Auth0 JWT, calls CCS to mint the `x-context-token`, injects a fresh `x-correlation-id`, and routes to the per-surface BFF. The BFF translates surface semantics into a capability string and is the only caller of `POST /dispatch`. The broker resolves, rate-limits, and dispatches.
